text: Earth's equatorial surface moves at roughly 1,670 km/h due to rotation
source: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, Earth Fact Sheet (equatorial rotation velocity about 1,674 km/h)

text: Angular momentum is conserved and cannot simply disappear
as_written: angular momentum does not simply vanish
source: Conservation of angular momentum, classical mechanics (Noether's theorem)

text: Foucault demonstrated Earth's rotation with a pendulum at the Panthéon in Paris in 1851
as_written: In 1851, the French physicist Léon Foucault hung a heavy ball
source: Foucault, Comptes Rendus de l'Académie des Sciences, 1851; Musée des Arts et Métiers

text: At Paris's latitude a Foucault pendulum's swing plane turns about 11.3 degrees per hour
source: Derived: sidereal rate 15.04 degrees per hour times sine of latitude 48.86 degrees

text: A full turn of the swing plane at Paris takes about 32 hours
source: Derived: 360 degrees divided by 11.3 degrees per hour

text: Earth's sidereal rotation period is 23 h 56 min 4 s
source: IERS / US Naval Observatory (sidereal day 23 h 56 m 4.09 s)

text: The sidereal day is about four minutes shorter than the 24-hour solar day
as_written: about four minutes shorter than the 24 hours
source: Derived from the sidereal day and the 24-hour mean solar day (IERS)

text: Earth's equatorial circumference is about 40,075 km
source: WGS 84 ellipsoid; NASA Earth Fact Sheet

text: London's rotational speed is about 1,040 km/h
source: Derived: equatorial speed times cosine of London's latitude, 51.5 degrees north

text: Equatorial rotation speed is about 465 m/s
source: NASA Goddard Earth Fact Sheet (equatorial rotation velocity 465.1 m/s)

text: Speed of sound at 15 °C is about 340 m/s
source: ISO 2533 / ICAO International Standard Atmosphere (340.3 m/s at 15 °C)

text: 465 m/s is about 1.4 times the speed of sound
as_written: roughly 1.4 times the speed of sound
source: Derived: 465 divided by 340.3

text: Strongest surface wind gust recorded by a weather station is 408 km/h at Barrow Island during Tropical Cyclone Olivia in 1996
as_written: 408 kilometres per hour, on Barrow Island in Australia, during Tropical Cyclone Olivia in 1996
source: World Meteorological Organization Weather and Climate Extremes Archive, 2010 ruling (113.3 m/s)

text: 1,670 km/h is about four times the record gust
as_written: about four times faster than that
source: Derived: 1,674 divided by 408

text: Dynamic pressure of a 465 m/s wind at sea-level density is about 130 kPa
source: Derived: half times 1.225 kg/m3 (ICAO standard sea-level density) times 465 squared

text: Standard sea-level air pressure is about 101 kPa
source: ICAO International Standard Atmosphere (101.325 kPa)

text: Half of the atmosphere's mass lies below about 5.5 km
source: NASA Glenn Research Center / US Standard Atmosphere 1976

text: At 45 degrees latitude the rotation speed is about 1,180 km/h
source: Derived: equatorial speed times cosine of 45 degrees

text: Speed of sound at 15 °C is about 1,225 km/h
source: ICAO International Standard Atmosphere (340.3 m/s)

text: Oceans cover about 71 percent of Earth's surface
source: NOAA National Ocean Service

text: Average ocean depth is about 3,700 m
source: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, ETOPO (mean depth about 3,688 m)

text: A tsunami crosses the deep ocean at roughly 800 km/h
source: NOAA Center for Tsunami Research / National Weather Service tsunami safety materials

text: Earth's rotational kinetic energy is about 2 x 10^29 joules
source: Derived: half times moment of inertia 8.04 x 10^37 kg m2 times angular velocity 7.292 x 10^-5 rad/s squared (IERS values)

text: World primary energy use is roughly 6 x 10^20 joules per year
as_written: about 6 times 10 to the 20 joules in a year
source: Energy Institute Statistical Review of World Energy (about 600 exajoules per year)

text: Rotational energy equals more than 300 million years of present world energy use
source: Derived: 2.1 x 10^29 J divided by 6 x 10^20 J per year

text: Normal apparent solar motion is 15 degrees per hour
source: Derived: 360 degrees divided by 24 hours

text: Without rotation the Sun shifts just under one degree per day
as_written: just under one degree per day
source: Derived: 360 degrees divided by 365.25 days

text: The Sun's angular diameter is about half a degree
source: NASA Sun Fact Sheet (mean angular diameter about 0.53 degrees)

text: The Sun would take about 13 hours to move its own width
source: Derived: 0.53 degrees divided by 0.986 degrees per day

text: Daylight and night each last about half a year at the equator
source: Derived: half of a 365.25-day solar day

text: Venus's sunrise-to-sunrise day is about 117 Earth days
source: NASA Venus Fact Sheet (solar day 116.75 Earth days)

text: Mercury's solar day is 176 Earth days
source: NASA Mercury Fact Sheet

text: The Moon's solar day is about 29.5 Earth days
source: NASA Moon Fact Sheet (synodic period 29.53 days)

text: Lunar equatorial surface reaches about 127 °C by day and falls to about minus 173 °C at night
as_written: about 127 degrees Celsius in the afternoon and falls to about minus 173 at night
source: NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Diviner instrument results; NASA Moon Fact Sheet

text: Hurricanes almost never form within about 5 degrees latitude of the equator because the Coriolis effect is too weak
as_written: within about 5 degrees of the equator
source: NOAA Atlantic Oceanographic and Meteorological Laboratory, Hurricane Research Division FAQ

text: Held and Hou's 1980 theory shows the Hadley circulation extends toward the poles on slowly rotating planets
as_written: A classic 1980 calculation by Isaac Held and Arthur Hou
source: Held and Hou, Journal of the Atmospheric Sciences, 1980

text: The Florida Current carries about 30 million cubic metres of water per second
as_written: about 30 million cubic metres of water every second
source: NOAA AOML Florida Current cable transport measurements (about 32 Sverdrups)

text: Global river discharge is under 1.5 million cubic metres per second, so the Gulf Stream exceeds it more than twenty times
as_written: more than twenty times the flow of every river on Earth combined
source: Dai and Trenberth 2002, Journal of Hydrometeorology (about 37,000 cubic km per year)

text: Stommel explained western boundary currents as a consequence of Earth's rotation in 1948
as_written: The oceanographer Henry Stommel showed in 1948
source: Stommel, Transactions of the American Geophysical Union, 1948

text: Earth's equatorial radius is 6,378 km
Earth's polar radius is 6,357 km
The equatorial bulge is about 21 km
source: Derived from WGS 84 radii

text: Removing rotation would shift sea level by kilometres; an order-of-magnitude estimate, not a precise value
source: Order-of-magnitude estimate derived from the roughly 21 km rotational flattening in WGS 84

text: Scandinavia is still rising from post-glacial rebound after ice melted roughly ten thousand years ago
source: Fennoscandian post-glacial rebound, e.g. BIFROST GPS project; Peltier glacial isostatic adjustment reviews

text: A non-rotating Earth would see the Sun move eastward among the stars, so it would rise in the west
as_written: It rises in the west and sets in the east, once a year
source: Derived from the Sun's apparent eastward annual motion along the ecliptic

text: Venus's retrograde spin makes the Sun rise in the west
as_written: Venus already does something like this
source: NASA Venus Fact Sheet (retrograde rotation, 243 days)

text: The terminator moves about 110 km per day at the equator, about 4.6 km/h
as_written: about 110 kilometres per day, which is about 4.6 kilometres per hour
source: Derived: 111.3 km per degree times 0.986 degrees per day

text: The outer core begins nearly 3,000 km down
as_written: Nearly three thousand kilometres under your feet
source: USGS; PREM, Dziewonski and Anderson 1981 (core-mantle boundary at about 2,890 km)

text: The outer core is about 2,260 km thick
source: PREM, Dziewonski and Anderson 1981 (2,890 km to 5,150 km depth)

text: Surface magnetic field strength is about 25 to 65 microtesla
source: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, World Magnetic Model

text: Mars lost its global magnetic field billions of years ago
as_written: Mars lost its global magnetic field billions of years ago
source: Acuña et al. 1999, Science (Mars Global Surveyor magnetometer)

text: Mars's surface pressure is about 160 times lower than Earth's
source: NASA Mars Fact Sheet (about 6.36 mbar vs 1,014 mbar)

text: MAVEN has measured the solar wind stripping gas from Mars's upper atmosphere
as_written: NASA's MAVEN spacecraft has measured the solar wind still stripping gas
source: Jakosky et al. 2015, Science; NASA MAVEN mission

text: The SI second is defined as 9,192,631,770 cycles of caesium-133 radiation
source: BIPM SI Brochure

text: 27 leap seconds have been added since 1972
source: IERS Bulletin C

text: In 2022 the General Conference on Weights and Measures resolved to stop leap seconds by 2035
as_written: in 2022 the world's measurement authorities agreed to stop doing that by 2035
source: 27th CGPM, November 2022, Resolution 4

text: Human intrinsic circadian period averages about 24 h 11 min
source: Czeisler et al. 1999, Science 284:2177

text: At the North Pole the Sun stays above the horizon for about six months
as_written: at the North Pole the sun stays up about six months each year
source: US Naval Observatory; NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory solar calculations

text: Joshi, Haberle and Reynolds found about 0.1 bar of atmosphere prevents atmospheric collapse on planets with a permanent night side
as_written: a surface pressure of only about 0.1 bar
source: Joshi, Haberle and Reynolds 1997, Icarus 129:450

text: Earth's surface pressure is about ten times 0.1 bar
as_written: Earth's air is about ten times thicker than that
source: Standard atmosphere, 1.013 bar

text: Cloud feedback on slowly rotating planets can extend habitability to higher sunlight levels
as_written: In 2013, Jun Yang, Nicolas Cowan and Dorian Abbot
source: Yang, Cowan and Abbot 2013, Astrophysical Journal Letters 771:L45

text: The eyeball climate state is a patch of open ocean ringed by ice
source: Pierrehumbert 2011, Astrophysical Journal Letters 726:L8

text: The twilight band of tide-locked planets is considered a promising habitat
as_written: the twilight band between them is a promising place for life
source: Pierrehumbert and Hammond 2019, Annual Review of Fluid Mechanics

text: Tidal friction lengthens the day by about 1.8 ms per century
source: Stephenson, Morrison and Hohenkerk 2016, Proceedings of the Royal Society A

text: The Moon recedes at about 3.8 cm per year, measured by lunar laser ranging
source: Apollo Lunar Laser Ranging retroreflectors; Williams and Boggs lunar laser ranging analyses

text: Devonian corals record roughly 400 days per year about 380 million years ago
source: Wells 1963, Nature 197:948

text: The day was about 18.7 hours long 1.4 billion years ago
source: Meyers and Malinverno 2018, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (Xiamaling Formation)

text: After the Moon-forming impact the day may have been two to five hours
as_written: somewhere between two and five hours
source: Ćuk and Stewart 2012, Science; Canup 2012, Science

text: The Moon's sidereal orbital period is 27.3 days
source: NASA Moon Fact Sheet (sidereal period 27.32 days)

text: High tides would come about half a sidereal month apart, around 13.7 days
source: Derived: half of 27.3 days

text: Tidal torque on a slowly spinning planet speeds its spin in the direction of the satellite's orbit and moves the satellite inward; the Sun's tides act the same way
as_written: twists the Earth gently forward, in the same direction the Moon orbits
source: Standard tidal evolution theory, e.g. Murray and Dermott, Solar System Dynamics
